chief_complaint: excruciating electric shock pain radiating down posterior leg below knee, numbness, and positive straight leg raise (L5/S1 Lumbar Radiculopathy)
hpi_details: 35M warehouse worker presents with 3 weeks of severe lower back pain and sharp, burning, `electric shock-like` pain shooting down the back of his left buttock, down the posterior thigh, through the calf, and into the outer border of his left foot and little toe. Pain started abruptly after lifting a 75-pound crate while twisting. Pain is aggravated dramatically by sitting, coughing, sneezing, or bending forward, and relieved slightly by lying flat on his back with pillows under his knees. Reports mild numbness along the outer edge of his left foot.
ideas: in severe shooting leg pain and unable to sit in a chair or drive to work
concerns: terrified he needs major emergency spine fusion surgery right away
expectations: wants MRI scan immediately, physical therapy, and strong nerve pain medication

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes conservative therapy with NSAIDs, neuropathic agents, and directional preference physical therapy while remaining active, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: excruciating electric shock pain radiating down posterior leg below knee, numbness, and positive straight leg raise (L5/S1 Lumbar Radiculopathy)

Key HPI features: 35M warehouse worker presents with 3 weeks of severe lower back pain and sharp, burning, `electric shock-like` pain shooting down the back of his left buttock, down the posterior thigh, through the calf, and into the outer border of his left foot and little toe. Pain started abruptly after lifting a 75-pound crate while twisting. Pain is aggravated dramatically by sitting, coughing, sneezing, or bending forward, and relieved slightly by lying flat on his back with pillows under his knees. Reports mild numbness along the outer edge of his left foot.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 78, BP 124/80. Lumbar spine exam shows loss of normal lordosis with paraspinal muscle spasm. Straight Leg Raise (SLR / Lasegue sign) is strongly POSITIVE on the left side at 35 degrees (reproducing sharp shooting pain down the leg below the knee; crossed straight leg raise is negative). Neurological examination of lower extremities reveals: 1. Motor: Ankle Plantarflexion (S1 - Gastrocnemius/Soleus tested via single-leg heel raises) shows mild weakness 4/5; Ankle Dorsiflexion (L4/L5) and Great Toe Extension (L5) are completely normal 5/5. 2. Reflexes: Left Achilles tendon reflex (S1) is ABSENT (0/4), right Achilles is normal 2+; bilateral patellar reflexes (L4) intact. 3. Sensory: hypoesthesia along the lateral aspect of the left foot and 5th toe (S1 dermatome). NO saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence, or bilateral leg weakness (excluding Cauda Equina Syndrome).
Relevant background/PMH: No prior lumbar issues
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Lumbar spinal stenosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence).
management_principles: Conservative PM&R management (First line for acute radiculopathy without progressive motor deficit or cauda equina syndrome, as >80% resolve spontaneously over 6-8 weeks via disc resorption): initiate short-course NSAIDs (Meloxicam 15 mg daily) combined with a neuropathic agent (Gabapentin 300 mg PO TID or Pregabalin 75 mg BID)
Physical Therapy: prescribe directional preference physical therapy (McKenzie extension exercises, core stabilization, and neural mobilization)
Strongly advise against strict bed rest; encourage remaining active within pain tolerance
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 35M presenting with acute unilateral sciatica / radicular pain following mechanical flexion-rotation lifting strain, distribution classic for S1 root compression.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 78, BP 124/80. Lumbar spine exam shows loss of normal lordosis with paraspinal muscle spasm. Straight Leg Raise (SLR / Lasegue sign) is strongly POSITIVE on the left side at 35 degrees (reproducing sharp shooting pain down the leg below the knee; crossed straight leg raise is negative). Neurological examination of lower extremities reveals: 1. Motor: Ankle Plantarflexion (S1 - Gastrocnemius/Soleus tested via single-leg heel raises) shows mild weakness 4/5; Ankle Dorsiflexion (L4/L5) and Great Toe Extension (L5) are completely normal 5/5. 2. Reflexes: Left Achilles tendon reflex (S1) is ABSENT (0/4), right Achilles is normal 2+; bilateral patellar reflexes (L4) intact. 3. Sensory: hypoesthesia along the lateral aspect of the left foot and 5th toe (S1 dermatome). NO saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence, or bilateral leg weakness (excluding Cauda Equina Syndrome).
reference_soap.assessment: Left S1 Lumbar Radiculopathy secondary to acute L5-S1 Posterolateral Herniated Nucleus Pulposus (Disc Herniation).
reference_soap.plan: In the absence of cauda equina features or progressive motor deficit, begin conservative care with activity within tolerance and rehabilitation-guided directional-preference, core, and neural-mobility exercises; avoid prolonged bed rest. Analgesics should be selected only after renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, sedating-medication, and other safety review. Obtain urgent assessment for saddle sensory change, bowel/bladder dysfunction, or progressive weakness. MRI, epidural injection, and surgical referral are conditional on the examination, duration/severity, response to conservative care, and specialist assessment.

learning_objectives: Correlate specific lumbar nerve root compression levels with their signature dermatomal sensory loss, myotomal motor weakness, and reflex changes (L4: anterior thigh/knee pain, quadriceps/ankle dorsiflexion weakness, diminished patellar reflex; L5: lateral leg/dorsal foot pain, great toe extension weakness EHL, normal reflexes; S1: posterior thigh/calf/lateral foot pain, ankle plantarflexion weakness, diminished/absent Achilles reflex)

Perform and interpret provocative nerve root tension tests including Straight Leg Raise (SLR sensitive for L4-S1 between 30-70 degrees) and Crossed Straight Leg Raise (highly specific for large central/axillary disc herniations)

Enforce evidence-based clinical guidelines recommending 6 to 8 weeks of conservative PM&R management (McKenzie physical therapy, NSAIDs, neuropathic drugs) prior to ordering lumbar MRI or surgical referral in the absence of red flags

Identify absolute surgical emergencies / red flags requiring STAT lumbar MRI and urgent neurosurgical decompression (Cauda Equina Syndrome: saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder retention or incontinence, progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness)

teaching.one_liner: Compression or inflammation of a lumbar nerve root causing sharp radiating leg pain, numbness, and motor weakness.
red_flags: Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence)

must_ask.say: Does the pain shoot down past your knee into your foot or toes?
Does coughing, sneezing, or sitting down make the leg pain much worse?
Have you noticed any numbness around your buttocks or loss of bowel or bladder control?
Does raising your straight leg while lying flat trigger the shooting pain?
Do you feel weakness when walking on your heels or toes?

history.answer: I've had terrible lower back pain for the past three weeks, and an electric shock pain keeps shooting all the way down my left leg into my foot.
It starts in my lower back and left buttock, shoots down the back of my thigh and calf, and goes right into the outer edge of my left foot and pinky toe.
It started suddenly three weeks ago when I lifted a heavy 75-pound crate at work while twisting my body.
It feels like a severe, sharp, burning electric shock shooting down my leg. It's an eight or nine out of ten at its worst.
Sitting in a chair, coughing, sneezing, or bending forward makes it flare up horribly. It eases up a bit only when I lie flat on my back with pillows propping up my knees.
It doesn't wake me up throbbing at night as long as I stay in that specific position with my knees bent, but any movement in bed can trigger a jolt.
My back is stiff for a few minutes when I first get out of bed, but it doesn't stay stiff for half an hour, and moving around doesn't make it better.
The outer border of my left foot and my little toe feel numb and tingly. My left ankle also feels a bit weak when I try to push off the ball of that foot.
No, the area between my legs and around my bottom feels completely normal. I have normal control over my bladder and bowels with no accidents or trouble going.

history.answer: Bending forward definitely makes the shooting pain much worse, and walking is painful, but sitting down doesn't make it better—sitting is actually the worst position.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/80 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and temperature 36.8°C.

Loss of normal lumbar lordosis with left paraspinal muscle spasm; straight leg raise test on the left is positive at 35 degrees reproducing sharp shooting leg pain below the knee, while crossed straight leg raise is negative.
Lumbar forward flexion and extension are markedly restricted due to pain, while lateral bending is mildly limited on the left.
Left ankle plantarflexion strength is 4/5 with difficulty performing single-leg heel raises, while ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension are 5/5 bilaterally.
Left Achilles tendon reflex is absent (0/4), right Achilles reflex is normal (2+), and bilateral patellar reflexes are intact (2+).
Hypoesthesia to light touch is present along the lateral border of the left foot and fifth toe, with intact sensation in all other lower extremity dermatomes.
Normal perianal sensation, intact anal wink, and normal resting and voluntary anal sphincter tone.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on either side.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, with no palpable pulsatile abdominal aortic mass or organomegaly.
Antalgic gait favoring the left leg with inability to perform repeated toe walking on the left side, but normal heel walking.
